newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-ENI shares surge after 2nd stage sell-off.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-ENI shares surge after 2nd stage sell-off.

text.p: Shares in Italy's state-controlled ENI surged on the Milan stock exchange on Monday when trading started after a second tranche sale of the oil and gas giant, seen by traders as an unqualified success.

"The sale has been a major, if predictable, success," said Oriano Moro, equity trader at Milan brokers Gestnord. "Its success had already been discounted. ENI is a well-liked stock, you have to have it in your portfolio," he added.
At midsession, ENI shares were quoted nearly one percent up at 7,230 lire after an opening 7,200 and day's high of 7,315 lire. The all-share stock index was up a modest 0.23 percent.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said at the weekend that the Treasury had pulled off Italy's largest privatisation so far with the sale of some 14 percent in ENI.
He said Italy raised at least 7.7 trillion lire ($5 billion) from the second tranche sale of 1.1 billion ENI shares which closed on Friday.
ENI, also listed in New York and London, is already the largest publicly traded company in Italy and the sixth largest publicly traded oil and gas company in the world.

Institutional investors were allocated 400 million ordinary shares, paying 7,161 lire per share -- Friday's official price on the Milan bourse. Retail investors were allocated 700 million shares at a discounted price of 6,910 lire per share.

"This was the biggest share offer yet seen in Italy, the biggest second tranche placement ever seen in Europe and the largest fully-paid placement in the world," Ciampi told a news conference on Saturday.

"The private investor should be well suited with the 6,910 lire price, and why sell when they get a one-for-10 bonus share if they hold on to the stock for a year," Moro said. "ENI could be one of the best performing stocks of 1997," he added.

The overall value of the flotation looks set to rise thanks to a reserve of 165 million shares which will be offered to institutions over the next month, under an over-allotment, or "green shoe", option, drawn up in case of heavy demand.
Ciampi said that if all the additional stock was sold, the Treasury would make 8.88 trillion lire from the second tranche sale, leaving the Treasury with a 69 percent stake in ENI.
The Treasury placed an initial 15 percent of ENI on the market last November at 5,250 lire per share. ENI shares hit a high of 7,925 lire on July 2.

It planned to sell just 700 million shares in the second tranche offering, with 250 million of these earmarked for small Italian investors. But heavy demand from this sector forced the Treasury to hike its offer last week by some 57 percent.
"The Treasury's strategy has worked well, keeping secret the final overall offer until the last moment," said Marco Nascimbeni, head of operations at Carnegie Italia brokers.
"It has wanted to place as many shares as possible with private investors who will no doubt hold on to their shares and institutional investors will get less than they asked for."
The Treasury said the institutional offering had been oversubscribed by three times. Allocations have yet to be set.

Some 383,000 small investors were involved, double the size seen in the first tranche sale. "But this is still a very small percentage of the Italian public. It will take some time to get such savers really interested in stocks," Nascimbeni said.
Some 42,000 ENI employees, who were offered especially favourable terms, had applied for around 84 million shares, and now have over one percent of ENI stock. ($1 = 1,522 lire)
